summary: Rolling red-clay uplands of the western North Carolina Piedmont, a little higher and cooler than most of the Piedmont. Winters give plenty of chill, but warm spells in late winter push apples into bloom around dogwood time, so a frost on open blossom is the usual spring risk. Summers are long, hot and humid, which makes summer fruit rots, not cold, the main limit.
apple_culture: Statesville sits just south-east of the Brushy Mountains, North Carolina's old Piedmont apple belt in Alexander and Wilkes counties (Taylorsville calls itself Apple Town; North Wilkesboro holds the Brushy Mountain Apple Festival each October). Iredell farms kept seedling and grafted home orchards, and heirloom hunters have found old local apples such as Red Potts, Phifer and Vandevere June around the town.
pests_diseases: Bitter rot and Glomerella leaf spot in the humid summer heat are the most serious problems, especially on Gala, Golden Delicious and their offspring; fire blight, cedar-apple rust (eastern red cedar is everywhere) and sooty blotch/flyspeck follow. Codling moth, plum curculio and brown marmorated stink bug are the main insects, and Phytophthora collar rot strikes trees on wet clay.
tips: Soil-test and work lime deep (to about 18 in) before planting, and choose a well-drained slope: the dense Iredell-series clays hold water. Pick rot- and blight-tolerant or proven southern heirloom varieties over Gala types, avoid MM.106 on clay, and keep a strict clean-up of mummies and cankers.
